name: Palatal expander

lead: A palatal expander widens the upper jaw by turning a screw in a fixed device, most commonly in children and adolescents aged about 8 to 18, to correct a narrow palate, crossbite and crowding. In looksmaxxing communities, expanders and MARPE are discussed for a broader smile and fuller midface, often alongside mewing.

Screw turns separate the two halves of the palate; new bone fills the gap and a retention period follows. Types include rapid (RME), slow, mini-implant-assisted (MARPE) and surgically assisted (SARPE) expansion. Trials focus on dental and airway outcomes in children; broader facial change in adults has not been tested in the sources reviewed.

paras: An orthodontist fits the device and the screw is turned on a set schedule, followed by months of retention. Older patients may use MARPE or surgical versions.
Speech changes, pain, a gap between front teeth, bone thinning and relapse are reported; MARPE and SARPE involve implants or surgery.

angle.text: A palatal expander widens the upper jaw, giving a broader dental arch and smile; in kids it is established orthodontics, and some adults hope for a fuller midface, sometimes alongside mewing. Facial change in adults has not been tested.

lead: A palatal expander is an orthodontic device used to widen the upper jaw so that upper and lower teeth fit together better, most commonly in children and adolescents aged about 8 to 18.[1] Types include rapid maxillary expansion (RME), slow expansion, mini-implant-assisted expansion (MARPE) and surgically assisted expansion (SARPE).[1] Orthodontists use expanders for a narrow upper jaw relative to the lower, posterior crossbite, cleft palate and crowding.[1]

In looksmaxxing communities the appeal is appearance-related. Members describe a wider palate as giving a broader smile, more room for teeth and, in their view, better midface support and nasal breathing, and they discuss expanders and MARPE alongside braces and mewing for people who consider their palate narrow.[2][3][4] Interest has been large on social platforms: a UK research proposal on TikTok's influence on patient acceptance of rapid maxillary expansion reported hundreds of millions of views for videos tagged jaw expander and palatal expander, and about 1.6 billion for orthodontic expander.[5]

Published research concerns mostly dental and airway outcomes in children and adolescents, together with a growing literature on MARPE in older adolescents and young adults. A 2025 meta-analysis of MARPE in mid-to-late adolescents and young adults pooled 17 studies and reported average midpalatal suture opening near 3 mm.[6] Orthodontic bodies and clinicians writing about online trends describe claims of broader facial reshaping in adults as lacking supporting evidence and recommend professional assessment.[7][8]
infobox: About 8 to 18; adults treated with implant or surgical assistance [1]
About 0.5 to 1 mm a day until crossbite corrects, then 3 to 6 months of retention [1]
Speech changes, pain, gap between front teeth, relapse [1]
Haas, Hyrax, bonded, quad helix, leaf expander, MARPE, SARPE [1]

paras: In rapid expansion a central screw is turned, typically about 0.5 to 1 mm a day, until a crossbite is corrected, and the device stays in for roughly three to six months while bone fills the gap, followed by retention.[1] Slow expansion turns about 1 mm per week over eight to ten weeks and is described as producing roughly equal skeletal and dental change.[1] Wikipedia says expansion is generally indicated when the upper jaw is about 4 mm or more narrower than the lower, measured at the first molars.[1]

MARPE anchors the appliance to the palatal bone with two to four mini-implants, so that force acts on bone rather than mainly on teeth, and is described as usable in young adults whose suture has fused; SARPE involves a surgeon cutting the suture.[1] A 2020 review describes MARPE as having extended the age limit of non-surgical maxillary expansion while noting that effectiveness, efficiency and stability needed reassessment as its use grew.[9] A 2023 scoping review comparing tooth-anchored, skeletal-anchored and leaf-type expanders reported meaningful skeletal widening of the palate with all devices studied.[10]

sections.h: How it is meant to improve appearance
paras: The direct benefits are functional and dental: correcting a crossbite, creating space for crowded teeth, and widening the upper arch so the smile fills the mouth.[1] Looksmaxxing posts extend this into facial claims, such as a wider palate supporting the midface, widening the nasal floor and improving nasal breathing.[2][3] Orthodontic literature reports that expansion opens several facial sutures and widens the nasal cavity, with changes concentrated in the front of the palate.[1][6]

Westcott reported applying mechanical force to the maxilla in 1859, and Emerson C. Angell published the first paper on palatal expansion in 1860 after placing a screw in a 14-year-old patient.[1] Wikipedia lists later developments: the Coffin spring (1877), opposition to Angell's approach from ADA president J. H. McQuillen (1889), the Haas expander (1956), the Hyrax (1968), the bonded type (1973) and the quad helix (1975).[1] MARPE emerged much later as a way of extending expansion to patients past the age of suture fusion.[9]

A meta-analysis of early correction of functional posterior crossbite found the quad helix more effective than expansion plates at increasing intermolar width, with greater relapse at about 5.6 years post-treatment. A randomised trial compared tooth-borne with tooth-bone-borne RME appliances over five years, and another compared clear aligners with RME in mixed dentition. A systematic review of bonded rapid palatal expanders in children reported slight increases in facial height of under 1 mm within six months, though most included studies had a high risk of bias.[11]
Older studies cited by Wikipedia (Krebs 1964, Stockfisch 1969, Linder Aronson 1979) found that one-third to one-half of expansion could be lost before the result stabilised.[1]

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis in Medicina Oral, Patología Oral y Cirugía Bucal covered 17 studies of MARPE in mid-to-late adolescents and young adults (392 patients for midpalatal data). It reported mean midpalatal suture opening of 2.99 mm and nasal cavity widening of 2.24 mm, found the pterygoid suture to be the only other suture significantly widened, and linked greater dental side effects to smaller midpalatal opening. The authors rated most studies at high risk of bias and called for randomised trials with larger samples and longer follow-up.[6]
Wikipedia states that adults can be treated but with more discomfort and longer treatment, and that most adults, especially men, may still need a surgical assist for consistent results.[1]

A systematic review reported that RME reduced the apnea-hypopnea index in children but rated the evidence low to very low and did not suggest it as an elective sleep apnea treatment. A network meta-analysis found RME alone was not associated with a significant AHI reduction, while combinations with adenotonsillectomy or mandibular advancement were. A randomised trial has compared RME with adenotonsillectomy.

Reported problems include speech difficulty, extra saliva, pain and headache when the screw is turned, tongue sores, a gap between the upper front teeth, bone thinning on the cheek side of the teeth and relapse.[1] MARPE adds placement of mini-implants, and SARPE involves a surgical cut and the usual surgical risks.[1][9] Wikipedia notes that the zygomatic buttress limits posterior expansion, so expansion occurs more at the front of the palate.[1]

looksmax.org threads ask whether an expander is worthwhile for a narrow or crowded palate,[2][3] whether it can widen the mandible,[12] and how it pairs with mewing.[4] One reply summarised rapid expansion as roughly 0.5 mm of widening a day over three to six months.[3]

Mewing, the tongue-posture practice associated with British orthodontist John Mew and his son Mike Mew, is the main related idea. Wikipedia says no credible research has demonstrated the efficacy of orthotropics, that the American Association of Orthodontists states there is no evidence mewing improves the jaw, and that Mike Mew was struck from the UK dental register in 2024.[8]

A February 2026 article in Dentistry by Grant McIntyre, a consultant orthodontist at the University of Dundee, describes a rise in online orthodontic misinformation and says internet-based schemes promising an improved facial appearance lack solid scientific support and pose health risks.[7] The NHS-registered TikTok study, sponsored by Cambridge University Hospitals, compares patients' willingness to accept orthodontic devices before and after watching related videos.[5]
Related topics include mewing and orthotropics, braces and clear aligners, jaw surgery (orthognathic and maxillary advancement), and nasal-breathing practices.[1][8]

Randomised and meta-analytic studies concern children's crossbite, appliance comparison, vertical changes and sleep-disordered breathing,[11] and a growing body of mostly low-quality studies covers MARPE in adolescents and young adults.[6] No studies found of palatal expanders used specifically for facial aesthetics in adults.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the expander is discussed as a way to widen a narrow palate, often paired with braces or mewing, with threads asking about adults, MARPE and mandible effects.[2][3][12][4]
